sentences.text: For much of the twentieth century, the bicycle was the most common way to cross a small city.
Workers rode to factories, children rode to school, and traders carried goods in baskets fixed to the front wheel.
As cars became cheaper, however, many towns widened their roads and removed the narrow lanes that cyclists had used.
In recent years, some councils have tried to reverse this trend by introducing shared bicycles.
A rider unlocks a bicycle with a phone, uses it for a short trip, and leaves it at any marked station.
The first schemes were often criticised because bicycles were left in the wrong places or damaged.
Later schemes placed stations closer together and charged a small fee for each trip, which reduced these problems.
Supporters of shared bicycles point to several benefits.
Short car journeys are replaced, so streets become quieter and the air in the centre becomes cleaner.
Local shops may also gain, because people on bicycles tend to stop more often than drivers do.
Critics reply that the schemes are expensive to run and that winter weather keeps many riders at home.
Planners agree that bicycles alone cannot solve a city's transport needs.
The most successful towns combine cycle lanes with buses and safe pavements, so that people can choose the best option for each journey.
In these places, the bicycle is no longer seen as old-fashioned but as one part of a modern network.

passages.title: How Rooftop Gardens Change a Building

sentences.text: Across many crowded cities, flat roofs are among the largest unused spaces.
A growing number of building owners are now covering them with soil and plants.
What was once a grey surface becomes a small field of grasses, herbs or vegetables.
The most immediate effect is on temperature.
A bare roof absorbs the summer sun and passes the heat into the rooms below.
A planted roof shades the building, and the water in the soil cools the air as it evaporates.
Residents of top-floor flats often notice that their rooms stay cooler without extra air conditioning.
Rooftop gardens also help with heavy rain.
On an ordinary roof, rainwater runs straight into the drains, which can overflow during a storm.
Soil holds much of this water and releases it slowly, so the drains have time to cope.
Building a garden on a roof is not simple, however.
Wet soil is heavy, and older roofs may need to be strengthened before any planting begins.
A waterproof layer must be laid beneath the soil to protect the building, and it has to be checked regularly.
These costs mean that rooftop gardens are more common on new buildings than on old ones.
For many residents, the greatest value of a rooftop garden is social.
Neighbours who rarely met in the stairwell now share tools, swap seeds and eat together on summer evenings.
Some gardens grow enough vegetables to supply a local café, giving the project a small income.

sentences.text: Few topics divide parents and teachers as sharply as homework.
Some see it as essential practice, while others believe it takes time that children need for rest and play.
In my view, the question is not whether homework should exist, but how much of it is useful.
A secondary school teacher I spoke to argued that short daily tasks help students remember what they learned in class.
She added that long assignments often end up being completed by parents rather than by the students themselves.
A university researcher who studies sleep pointed to a different problem.
According to him, teenagers who work late into the evening sleep less and concentrate poorly the next day.
A parents' group I visited had collected its own evidence.
Its members kept diaries for a month and found that homework often caused arguments at home.
They did not want homework removed; they wanted it to be clearer and shorter.
I believe these voices point to the same conclusion.
Homework works best when it is brief, closely linked to the lesson, and possible to finish without help.
Schools that set less but better homework may find that their students learn more, not less.
